Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Police tightened security at airports across Pakistan Thursday after receiving reports of a possible suicide attack at the international airport that serves Islamabad. Pakistan's capital was rocked by a suicide attack on the city's Marriott Hotel at the weekend. Officers emptied the parking lot at the Benazir Bhutto International Airport, on the outskirts of Islamabad, said Parvez George of the country's Civil Aviation Authority. Flights were going out of the airport, but police cleared the terminal building of the large crowds that usually gather to see relatives arrive or depart, George said. Muhammad Asghar of Islamabad Police told CNN that authorities placed the airport on high alert after intelligence reports indicated it was under threat of an attack. The country's capital city is on edge since a deadly blast Saturday night at the Marriott Hotel. The explosion killed more than 50 people, including two U.S. military personnel and the Czech ambassador to Pakistan. The bombing wounded more than 250 and sparked a fire that left the hotel in ruins. On Thursday, the Danish intelligence service said one of its employees, Karsten Krabbe, was among the victims of the blast. Krabbe, a 53-year-old married father of two, was a security adviser at the Danish Embassy in Islamabad, which was targeted by a suicide bomber in June. That attack killed six people and wounded more than 20. "Karsten Krabbe lost his life in a cowardly and ruthless terror attack," the Danish intelligence service said in a statement. Reacting to the Saturday's attack, the U.S. government barred employees from major hotels in several Pakistani cities, the U.S. Embassy in Pakistan said. The Embassy in Islamabad added Lahore on Wednesday to a list of three other cities in which U.S. personnel are no longer allowed to visit or stay in major hotels. The Embassy took the measures because of general security concerns, said spokesman Lou Fintor Thursday. He did not comment on a specific threat. In addition to the hotel restriction, the Embassy temporarily suspended visa and other routine consular services for Thursday and Friday. It said it will make available emergency services for U.S. citizens who need passports or are arrested. And an advisory reminded Americans in Pakistan to avoid crowds and demonstrations and to keep a "low profile." It said Americans should vary times and routes while traveling to avoid setting patterns. And it said a travel warning issued on August 7 still stands: U.S. citizens should defer nonessential travel to Pakistan due to continuing security concerns. -- CNN's Zein Basravi and Reza Sayah, and Journalist Nasir Habib contributed to this report .

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) — Police tightened security at airports across Pakistan on Thursday after receiving reports of a possible suicide attack at the international airport serving Islamabad.

Pakistan’s capital was shaken over the weekend by a suicide attack on the city’s Marriott Hotel.

Officers cleared the parking lot at Benazir Bhutto International Airport, located on the outskirts of Islamabad, said Parvez George of the country’s Civil Aviation Authority. Flights continued to depart from the airport, but police cleared the terminal building of the large crowds that typically gather to see relatives arrive or depart, George said.

Muhammad Asghar of Islamabad Police told CNN that authorities placed the airport on high alert after intelligence reports indicated it was under threat of an attack.

The capital has been on edge since Saturday night’s deadly blast at the Marriott Hotel. The explosion killed more than 50 people, including two U.S. military personnel and the Czech ambassador to Pakistan. The bombing also wounded more than 250 people and sparked a fire that left the hotel in ruins.

On Thursday, the Danish intelligence service said one of its employees, Karsten Krabbe, was among the victims of the blast. Krabbe, a 53-year-old married father of two, was a security adviser at the Danish Embassy in Islamabad, which was targeted by a suicide bomber in June. That attack killed six people and wounded more than 20.

“Karsten Krabbe lost his life in a cowardly and ruthless terror attack,” the Danish intelligence service said in a statement.

In response to Saturday’s attack, the U.S. government barred its employees from major hotels in several Pakistani cities, the U.S. Embassy in Pakistan said.

On Wednesday, the Embassy in Islamabad added Lahore to a list of three other cities where U.S. personnel are no longer permitted to visit or stay in major hotels. The Embassy took the measures because of general security concerns, spokesman Lou Fintor said Thursday. He did not comment on any specific threat.

In addition to the hotel restriction, the Embassy temporarily suspended visa and other routine consular services for Thursday and Friday. It said emergency services would remain available for U.S. citizens who need passports or who are arrested.

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) — Security was increased at airports throughout Pakistan on Thursday following reports warning of a potential suicide bombing at the international airport serving Islamabad.

The heightened precautions came just days after Pakistan’s capital was shaken by a suicide attack on the Marriott Hotel over the weekend.

At Benazir Bhutto International Airport, located on the outskirts of Islamabad, police cleared the parking area, according to Parvez George of Pakistan’s Civil Aviation Authority. Flights continued to operate from the airport, but officers removed the large groups of people who typically gather inside the terminal to greet or send off relatives, George said.

Muhammad Asghar of the Islamabad Police told CNN that officials put the airport on high alert after intelligence information suggested it faced a possible attack.

Islamabad has remained tense since Saturday night’s deadly bombing at the Marriott Hotel. More than 50 people were killed in the blast, among them two members of the U.S. military and the Czech ambassador to Pakistan. Over 250 others were injured, and the explosion triggered a fire that destroyed much of the hotel.

On Thursday, Denmark’s intelligence agency announced that one of its staff members, Karsten Krabbe, was also killed in the attack. Krabbe, 53, was married and had two children. He worked as a security adviser at the Danish Embassy in Islamabad, which had itself been struck by a suicide bomber in June. That earlier attack left six people dead and injured more than 20 others.

“Karsten Krabbe lost his life in a cowardly and ruthless terror attack,” the Danish intelligence service said in a statement.

In response to Saturday’s bombing, the U.S. government prohibited its employees from visiting major hotels in several Pakistani cities, the U.S. Embassy in Pakistan said.

On Wednesday, the U.S. Embassy in Islamabad added Lahore to a list of three other cities where American personnel are no longer permitted to stay at or enter major hotels. Embassy spokesman Lou Fintor said Thursday that the decision was based on broader security concerns, but he declined to discuss any particular threat.

Along with the hotel ban, the Embassy temporarily halted visa processing and other regular consular services for Thursday and Friday. It said emergency assistance would still be provided to U.S. citizens who need passports or who have been arrested.

An advisory also urged Americans in Pakistan to stay away from crowds and protests and to maintain a “low profile.” It advised U.S. citizens to change their travel times and routes so they do not establish predictable patterns.

The advisory further noted that a travel warning issued on August 7 remains in effect, urging U.S. citizens to postpone nonessential travel to Pakistan because of ongoing security concerns.

CNN’s Zein Basravi and Reza Sayah, along with journalist Nasir Habib, contributed to this report.

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan** — Pakistani authorities tightened security at Islamabad’s main airport after intelligence agencies warned of a possible suicide attack, police officials said, as the capital remained on edge following the deadly bombing of the Marriott Hotel.

Police increased patrols and deployed additional officers around Islamabad International Airport, with vehicles and passengers facing more intensive checks at entry points, according to security officials. Authorities also stepped up screening in surrounding areas and placed rapid-response units on alert.

The heightened security follows warnings that militants could be planning an attack using a suicide bomber, officials said. No specific group was immediately named in connection with the threat.

The alert comes in the aftermath of the massive truck bombing at the Marriott Hotel in Islamabad, an attack that killed dozens of people and wounded many more. The bombing, which left a large crater outside the hotel and set parts of the building ablaze, underscored the ability of militant groups to strike heavily guarded targets in the Pakistani capital.

Security has been increased across Islamabad since the Marriott attack, with police erecting additional checkpoints near government buildings, diplomatic missions, hotels and transport hubs.

Pakistani officials have said they are investigating links between the Marriott bombing and militant networks operating in the country’s tribal regions along the Afghan border, where al Qaeda and Taliban-linked fighters have long maintained a presence.

Airport operations were continuing, but passengers were advised to arrive early because of delays caused by security inspections. Officials said the measures would remain in place as long as the threat level remained elevated.

**CNN-style draft article**  
**September 22, 2008**

# Pakistan airports on alert after deadly Islamabad hotel bombing

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan** — Pakistani authorities placed major airports on heightened alert following the massive truck bombing at the Marriott Hotel in Islamabad, an attack that killed dozens of people and raised new fears about security in the country’s heavily guarded capital.

The blast, which struck Saturday evening outside the hotel’s front entrance, left a deep crater and set off a fire that engulfed much of the building. Officials said more than 50 people were killed and scores more injured in one of the deadliest attacks in Islamabad’s history.

Among the victims was **Karsten Krabbe**, a Danish citizen, according to officials and diplomatic sources. Foreign nationals were among those killed and wounded in the explosion, which targeted a hotel frequently used by diplomats, aid workers, journalists and visiting business travelers.

Security officials said airports in Islamabad, Lahore, Karachi and other major cities were operating under increased vigilance after the attack. Passengers faced tighter screening, additional vehicle checks and a heavier police and paramilitary presence around terminal entrances and access roads.

The bombing also prompted new security restrictions by foreign missions in Pakistan. The **U.S. Embassy in Islamabad** limited staff movements and warned American personnel to avoid hotels, restaurants and other public gathering places considered potential targets. Embassy officials urged U.S. citizens in Pakistan to remain alert, review personal security plans and monitor local developments.

The Marriott bombing came just hours after Pakistan’s new president, Asif Ali Zardari, addressed Parliament and vowed to fight terrorism. Investigators said the attacker drove an explosives-laden truck toward the hotel’s security barrier before detonating the vehicle. Surveillance footage showed guards attempting to stop the truck shortly before the blast.

Pakistani authorities said the size of the explosion suggested hundreds of kilograms of explosives were used. The fire that followed burned for hours, complicating rescue efforts and trapping some guests and staff inside the building.

No group immediately claimed responsibility, but officials said the attack bore the hallmarks of Islamist militant networks operating in Pakistan’s tribal areas near the Afghan border.

The bombing has intensified concerns about Pakistan’s stability and the ability of militants to strike high-profile targets despite heavy security. The Marriott, long regarded as one of Islamabad’s best-protected hotels, was located near government offices, foreign embassies and diplomatic residences.

Authorities said the investigation was continuing as rescue workers searched the damaged hotel and hospitals treated the wounded.

**Islamabad on edge after Marriott Hotel bombing; U.S. urges caution**

ISLAMABAD — Pakistan’s capital remained tense after the devastating suicide truck bombing at the Marriott Hotel, with security tightened around government buildings, diplomatic missions, major hotels and the airport as authorities warned of the possibility of further attacks.

The blast, which struck the heavily guarded hotel in central Islamabad, killed dozens of people and wounded many more. The attack left a crater outside the hotel, ignited a massive fire and shattered the sense of security in one of the capital’s most fortified districts, near Parliament, the presidency and several embassies.

Police said checkpoints had been reinforced across Islamabad and surrounding areas, with additional patrols deployed at entry points to the city.

“We are treating the capital as a high-risk zone,” a senior Islamabad police official said. “Security has been increased at all sensitive installations, hotels and public places, and we are checking vehicles more aggressively.”

Aviation authorities said operations at Islamabad’s airport were continuing, but passengers were being advised to arrive early because of heightened security screening on access roads and inside the terminal.

“Flights are operating, but security procedures have been tightened,” an aviation official said. “Travelers should expect delays because vehicles and baggage are being checked more thoroughly.”

The attack intensified concerns among foreign governments about the security situation in Pakistan, where militant violence has surged amid political instability and military operations against insurgent groups.

The U.S. State Department warned Americans to defer nonessential travel to Pakistan, citing the threat of extremist attacks against Western targets, government facilities and public places. U.S. officials also urged American citizens already in Pakistan to maintain a low profile, avoid large gatherings and exercise particular caution around hotels, restaurants, markets and places frequented by foreigners.

The U.S. Embassy in Islamabad said it was reviewing security arrangements and limiting some movements by personnel. Washington has periodically issued travel warnings for Pakistan because of bombings, kidnappings and attacks on civilian and government targets.

Pakistani investigators continued examining the Marriott blast site, including security camera footage and vehicle debris, to determine how the attacker managed to reach the hotel’s security barrier with a truck packed with explosives.

The Marriott had long been a prominent gathering place for Pakistani officials, foreign diplomats, aid workers and journalists. Its destruction sent a powerful message through the capital, where residents said the attack underscored the reach of militants despite layers of security.

“This was not just an attack on a hotel,” the police official said. “It was meant to create fear in the heart of Islamabad.”

counterfactuals.output:
**ISLAMABAD (Wire report) —** Pakistani authorities tightened security around airports, diplomatic missions, government buildings and major hotels after a series of terror warnings prompted evacuations, travel advisories and new movement restrictions for foreign personnel, officials said.

Police and paramilitary units were deployed at key intersections in Islamabad and other major cities, while security checks were intensified near airports, luxury hotels, foreign missions and places of worship. Authorities said the measures followed “credible threat information” but did not publicly identify a specific group or target.

At least one airport terminal was temporarily evacuated after a reported bomb threat, according to aviation and security officials. Passengers were moved to secure areas while bomb-disposal teams and sniffer dogs searched the premises. Flights were delayed during the sweep, but officials said no explosive device was immediately reported found and operations later resumed in phases.

The heightened alert came as Western embassies issued warnings to their citizens in Pakistan. The U.S. Embassy advised Americans to exercise increased vigilance and avoid crowded public areas, especially hotels, markets, government facilities and places of worship. In a separate internal restriction, U.S. government personnel were barred from visiting at least one major hotel in Islamabad because of what the embassy described as a possible threat.

Embassy officials said the hotel ban applied to official U.S. personnel and urged private American citizens to review their own security plans, maintain a low profile and monitor local media. Similar advisories from other diplomatic missions urged their nationals to avoid large gatherings and unnecessary travel in sensitive areas.

Pakistani police said security had been reinforced around diplomatic enclaves and foreign residences. Checkpoints were expanded on roads leading to Islamabad’s high-security Red Zone, which houses parliament, the Supreme Court, government offices and many embassies. Officers in armored vehicles were seen conducting random searches of cars and motorcycles.

Interior Ministry officials said provincial governments had been instructed to raise threat monitoring and coordinate with intelligence agencies. “All law-enforcement agencies are on alert,” one senior security official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to discuss threat assessments publicly.

The warnings followed a rise in militant violence in Pakistan, including attacks targeting police, military personnel and civilians. Authorities have blamed much of the recent violence on the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has increased attacks since ending a cease-fire with the government. Other extremist factions, including Islamic State-linked militants and separatist groups, have also claimed attacks in different parts of the country.

Officials said there were no immediate reports of casualties from the airport evacuations or hotel-related security alerts. However, casualty figures from recent militant incidents continued to be updated by local authorities as hospitals, police and rescue services reconciled reports from attack sites. Security officials said several police and military personnel had been killed or wounded in recent operations and militant attacks, while suspected militants were also reported killed in counterterrorism raids.

Hospitals in affected areas were placed on standby, and rescue agencies said ambulance crews had been told to remain prepared for possible emergencies. Authorities urged the public to report suspicious activity and avoid spreading unverified information on social media.

Pakistan has experienced periodic waves of militant violence despite large-scale military operations in former insurgent strongholds along the Afghan border. Officials say the security environment has become more volatile since the Taliban returned to power in neighboring Afghanistan, a development Islamabad says has allowed some militants greater freedom of movement. Afghan Taliban authorities deny allowing their territory to be used for attacks inside Pakistan.

The U.S. advisory underscored long-standing concerns about attacks on Western targets in Pakistan. Major hotels in Islamabad, Karachi, Lahore and Peshawar have previously been targeted or placed under heavy security because they are frequented by foreign diplomats, aid workers, journalists and business travelers.

Pakistani officials said the latest precautions were preventive and that there was no decision to close airports or diplomatic facilities nationwide. Still, passengers were advised to arrive early for flights because of additional screening, while residents of Islamabad reported longer waits at checkpoints and restricted access near sensitive installations.

Authorities said the heightened measures would remain in place until security agencies completed their review of the threat information.
